chunks.content: Introduction Breast cancer is a leading cause of death among female cancer patients and comprised 24% of all female cancers in Norway in 2022. The incidence of breast cancer has increased over the past decades, , and the relative survival has increased continuously due to earlier diagnosis and better treatment. , Unfortunately, surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormone treatment and other treatments alone or in combination may have detrimental effects to the daily life and well-being of many breast cancer survivors (BCS). Moreover, fatigue, memory complaints and pain may result in reduced ability to work, occupational concerns, struggle in returning to work, and risk of permanently leaving the labor force. – Compared with other cancers affecting women, breast cancer is more frequently diagnosed in the working age group (<65 years), and the negative consequence of reduced employment for the individual BCS may be substantial. Not only does discontinuation of employment result in financial instability, work and the workplace are also important for fostering social relationships, contributing to people’s quality of life, and they give meaning to life. Unfortunately, few longitudinal studies have examined employment outcomes among women diagnosed with cancer, – and few studies have included a matched control group. , , A Finnish study found that employment among BCS was reduced during the first 5 years following diagnosis, however earnings reductions were most severe during the first 2 years. A Dutch study found that BCS more often received disability benefits and lost their paid employment compared to the general population 5–10 years after diagnosis. A German study comparing patients whose primary diagnosis was breast cancer with matched controls from the general population found that nearly three times as many cancer patients had left their job compared to the reference group, and the probability of returning to work 6 years after surgery was only half of the reference group’s. However, they included patients up to 70 years of age, resulting in a substantially lower number of patients at follow-up since many reached the retirement age of 65 years during the study. Thus, inclusion of more patients below retirement age is warranted in future studies. Both health-related and socioeconomic factors negatively influence employment in BCS. , To our knowledge, only a few studies have assessed the effects of a wider variety of sociodemographic risk factors in a retrospective cohort study. Factors such as chemotherapy, cancer stage, older age and less accommodating employers are associated with reduced working hours, long-term disability, and early retirement in the short-term. However, a Dutch study showed that work related factors (e.g. type of contract, physically demanding jobs, and current work ability) were associated with adverse work outcomes 5–10 years after diagnosis, whereas clinical factors (e.g. surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy) were not. Importantly, recent studies have shown that the time needed to adapt and manage late effects of cancer treatment during the return-to-work period is a process that may last for several years. – Since many breast cancer patients are diagnosed relatively early in their life and are expected to live for many years, there is a need for studies with longer follow-up periods. In fact, only a few studies have addressed the influence of clinical and socioeconomic factors on long-term employment after diagnosis. , Thus, the influence of these factors after the first years remains largely unknown in many countries. Long-term studies should preferably apply a matched control group, reducing the influence of bias because of country specific labor market structures and inherent changes in employment rates within the country’s overall population. People with chronic diseases have reduced employment prospects compared to people without health challenges, in part because they have more difficulty re-entering the labor market, or they leave employment earlier. However, most studies of employment among BCS have focused on those working at the time of diagnosis. An important but little studied component of breast cancer is its role in reducing entry into employment among individuals not-working before cancer diagnosis. , Thus, it is important to include information regarding employment status at diagnosis because BCS in employment and BCS outside employment may not have the same likelihood of being in employment after cancer. The primary aim of this study was to investigate the likelihood of employment during the first 6 years after diagnosis among BCS and matched controls who were in employment at the time of diagnosis. The secondary aim was to investigate the likelihood of entry into employment within 6 years after diagnosis among BCS and matched controls who were not employed at the time of diagnosis. Design and methods Registries In this retrospective register-based cohort study, BCS were identified by use of the Cancer Registry of Norway, which is a comprehensive population-based registry with mandatory reporting. Norway has a universal, and largely free for all, health care system, thus the Cancer Registry encompasses virtually all Norwegian cancer patients. , Demographic data (e.g. age, gender, education) and work-related data (work contract, industry code) for BCS and controls were received from Statistics Norway. Data from the registries were linked through a personal identification number. Material In the Cancer Registry of Norway, we identified 10,454 new breast cancer cases (ICD-10 code C50 Malignant neoplasm of breast) diagnosed from 2004 through 2008 for all ages. We excluded patients with multiple cancers ( n = 1589), those who died during follow-up ( n = 1646), a small group of stage IV patients ( n = 32) and two male patients. Only BCS aged 30 through 55 years were included in the analyses; patients outside this age range ( n = 3451) were excluded for reasons described below. Self-employed individuals were not included in this study because it was impossible to ascertain whether self-employed individuals in fact were working at all or at different times during the year, for example, at the time of the cancer diagnosis. The age range of 30–55 years was chosen based on labor-force participation in general, and that breast cancer is most often diagnosed among people aged 40 and above. Among younger people, many may still be in education in their 20s. Early retirement increases from about 60 years of age and participants close to this age at the end of our follow-up may more likely choose to retire instead of making efforts to return to employment. By excluding BCS’ early retirement availability, the employment outcome should not be biased by this alternative. Each BCS was matched with two unique cancer free controls randomly extracted from the remaining general population (i.e. after the aforementioned exclusions). Controls had to be cancer free during follow-up (i.e. through 2014). Matching was based on age, education level and employment status at time of diagnosis. Our data allowed us to use exact matching, that is, BCS and controls were identical regarding the matching variables. Exact matching is the preferred matching method but can result in larger bias if there is a failure to match a large share of cases. We were able to match all selected BCS to identical controls, thus there was no selection bias on the matching variables. Controls were given a pseudo-diagnosis date according to their corresponding BCS’ diagnosis time. When controls were matched to a cancer case, they were blocked from being selected again. Some BCS ( N = 131) were excluded because of missing information on employment industry and/or sector, and a few controls ( N = 19) did not have valid information on industry, thus 19 BCS have only one control. The dataset ultimately included 3550 BCS and 7081 controls, who were followed from 2004/2008 through 2010/2014. The year of diagnosis (2004/2008; baseline) is labeled T 0 , the first year after diagnosis is labeled T 1 (2005/2009) and so on to T 6 (2010/2014). Thus, we followed up five pooled cohorts of BCS for a total of 6 years. Variables Employment was the dependent variable and for t 0 (baseline), it was defined as being registered with an employer within the 90 days prior to- and including the date of cancer diagnosis (e.g. if a BCS was diagnosed on December 31st 2004, then she had to have a valid work contract for October–December 2004). All employment contracts were included; thus employment includes both part-time and full-time employees as well as employees on temporary contracts. For the follow-up years ( t 1 – t 6 ), employment was similarly defined as having a valid contract within 90 days prior to the start of the given follow-up year (i.e. for t 2 : a valid employment contract in October–December 2006). Statistics The analyses included descriptive characteristics of the study population (BCS and controls), and overall share of BCS and controls in employment during follow-up according to employment status at time of diagnosis ( ). Differences in the share employed between BCS and controls were tested by means of t -tests. If our matching removed all observed and unobserved imbalances between BCS and controls, the differences between BCS and controls in are correct and unbiased. However, this is both uncertain and probably unlikely. To investigate imbalances between BCS and controls we included the variables described above in our subsequent analyses. Due to our initial exact matching, BCS and controls had very similar family, industry and sector characteristics at the time of diagnosis. Thus, on a group level, BCS and controls were also closely matched on family type, industry and sector at t 0 . Separate multiple logistic regression models for each year during follow-up ( t 1 through t 6 ) were estimated for two BCS groups: (i) employed at diagnosis or (ii) not employed at diagnosis, and their respective controls. The advantage of this approach is that BCS or controls temporarily not in employment at a given time during follow-up were retained if they returned to employment at a later stage. In the multiple logistic regression results: we presented the average marginal effects for each covariate, which indicates the average change in the predicted probability of the outcome measure (e.g. employment at t 6 ), while keeping the values of all the other covariates constant across all observations in the sample. Stata’s “margins” command was used to estimate the standard errors and confidence intervals (CIs) for the marginal effects shown in the and . Logistic regression tables results are presented in Supplemental Files 1 and 2 . The study included treatment variables: surgery , chemotherapy , radiation , and hormone therapy . However, in a model with cancer stage, these treatment variables were not significant due to high correlation with cancer stage (multicollinearity). This is because cancer stage (to a certain extent) determines treatment. The treatment variables were thus excluded from our final analysis. Matching variables were included in our analyses, thus adjusting for group residual covariate imbalances , and enabling us to check whether the likelihood of employment post-diagnosis between BCS compared to controls varied by age and education level; we found no significant interaction effects (not shown). All analyses were performed in Stata/SE 16.1 for Windows. This manuscript was prepared following the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) statement ( Supplemental File 3 ). The age of the BCS were on average 47.6 years when diagnosed, more than half (53%) of them were living with a spouse/partner and children; and the most common educational level was secondary education (42%) followed by lower-level university education (30.7%), basic education (20.2%) and higher-level university education (7.2%). investigate the factors affecting employment up to 6 years after diagnosis among BCS of working age (30–55 years) in Norway. The results of this nationwide study have shown sustained lower employment in BCS employed and not employed at baseline, compared to controls over a 6-year period after diagnosis. Furthermore, our study suggests that cancer stage (among BCS compared to controls) and sociodemographic factors (among BCS and controls) such as caring for children and being educated are significant determinants of employment. Reduced ability to work has been shown to be higher among BCS than among non-cancer groups and can be a consequence of treatment-related late effects and the psychological burden of cancer diagnosis. , A reduction in the share of employed BCS found in our study confirms previous research. , , We found that between 72 and 74 percent of BCS were employed 1–6 years after diagnosis. This is in line with a meta-analysis reporting a 28% higher non-employment rate among BCS compared to a control population. In comparison, a prospective cohort study of Danish BCS reported 81% employment 2 years after diagnosis; however, they included older cancer survivors who received early retirement- or anticipatory pension. Future studies should also consider whether patients received social benefits or pensions during the study period given that a possible mechanism behind high unemployment rate among cancer survivors is a higher disability rate. Numerous barriers and facilitators that could have a negative impact negatively on employment following BC diagnosis have been identified. They include factors such as age, lack of social support, comorbidities, treatment modalities, education and income. In our study, severe cancer stage was not associated with lower likelihood of employment. This finding is in contrast with previous studies showing that women with advanced stages have lower employment rates after BC diagnosis compared to those with other stages of cancer. , , Normally, BCS with advanced stage diagnosis may suffer from side effects that may require continued treatment and can limit employment or lead to disability. Oncological surgery has been shown to be associated with long-term adverse effects, and one study found that BCS who had undergone a mastectomy were more likely to have stopped working Seven months post- diagnosis. A French study showed that ongoing chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy was associated with lower employment 5 years after diagnosis. However, the present study only included BCS who were alive 6 years after diagnosis, thus the BCS included may have been in better health compared to patients in previous studies. Consistent with prior studies, , the present study showed that being educated increased the likelihood of employment. Education level has been shown to be stratified by the type of job, whereby low educated patients were more likely to work as manual laborers and thus engage in heavy lifting jobs resulting in experiences of fatigue. This study did not examine the conditional effects involving level of education and employment sector; but we found significant group differences in the effect of education on employment net of employment sector. In the current study BCS and controls with children showed a greater likelihood of employment compared to BCS and controls without children. This is in line with numerous studies that have found that women with children return to employment more often compared to women without children, which could be due to financial necessity. , Our study did not differentiate between for example, having young/dependent versus adult/independent children. This is an area that should be examined in future studies; for example, financial and other forms of support from adult children might reduce the financial strain experienced by BCS and the attendant pressure to prematurely return to work. BCS in this study could be out of employment for different reasons, with some of them potentially being out of the labor force due to cancer. However, it should be noted that the current study included a relatively healthy group of BCS by excluding those who had more than one cancer diagnosis. In addition, BCS who died during follow-up were not included in the analyses. It is likely that breast cancer patients with the most severe illness died during the study period. Thus, our study addressed BCS with a long life-expectancy following diagnosis. Reports from Norway have shown that in the general population, employment in Norway peaks around the age of 40–50 years Norway. Since BCS up to 55 years were included, only a few may have chosen early retirement due to reassessment of their priorities following a cancer disease. Therefore, our participants were also rather young compared to other comparable studies, with a mean age of 47.6 years at baseline. Therefore, our participants were also rather young compared to other comparable studies, with a mean age of 47.6 years at baseline. However, it might be that the physical and psychological impact of the disease and treatment affected the patients’ employment seeking behavior. At later ages, the employment rate for both genders in the general population start decreasing and the rate of sickness absences and disability pensions start increasing. These factors may also explain the decrease in employment over time among the controls in the present study. It should also be noted that differences in results between studies may be explained by differences in the definition of employment. They may also be due to studies being conducted in countries with a diversity of social security systems. By international comparison, the employment rate is very high in Norway, both for men and women. One important factor behind the well-functioning Norwegian labor market is the so-called “tripartism.” This involves cooperation amongst unions, employers and the government for a more inclusive working life through the inclusive workplace agreement, which is aimed at helping achieve high employment and mobilizing the workforce by preventing and reducing sick leave and withdrawal from working life. , It should also be noted that employment rates and education levels are high for Norwegian women compared to those in other countries; and the generosity of the welfare state in Norway, which makes it possible to combine family life and work, has contributed to the high participation rate of women. , In countries with lower female employment rates and less supportive welfare systems, the differences in employment between BCS and controls may be more substantial compared to our findings. However, our findings corroborate overall findings from various welfare systems and labor markets, but it should be noted that results may vary substantially according to welfare regime. Strength and limitations A strength of the study was the use of registry-based individual level measures of employment, with high validity and completeness, allowing the selection of data according to inclusion criteria. The longitudinal design and inclusion of a control group of age-matched women was another strength of the study. Our use of a control group allowed us to account for sociodemographic factors (age, education, family type, employment industry) that may have influenced employment participation during the study period. Findings from our study should be interpreted in light of its limitations. Although we matched breast cancer survivors (BCS) and controls on key sociodemographic variables, including educational level and employment status, unobserved differences may still exist—particularly with regard to lifestyle-related factors such as smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, obesity, and hormone use. These factors are known to influence both cancer risk and employment outcomes, but were not available in our dataset. While education is a strong proxy for many health-related behaviors, residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Nonetheless, the use of a matched control group without a cancer diagnosis during the study period strengthens the internal validity of our comparisons, as it allows us to isolate the potential impact of cancer and its treatment on employment outcomes. The present study did not account for working hours, but included all employment, both part-time and full-time. BCS may work reduced hours to a larger extent than controls, but this was not addressed here. Future studies may want to investigate whether there are differences in working hours between BCS and controls. Previous studies have shown that BCS may experience both reduced and increased earnings, suggesting that working hours may both increase and decrease following a breast cancer diagnosis. These variations may reflect individual coping strategies, workplace accommodations, or economic necessity, and could have important implications for understanding the full impact of breast cancer on labor market participation. Additionally, our study did not include information regarding employment before diagnosis. A study from Denmark showed that the duration of unemployment before diagnosis was the most important determinant of unemployment following cancer diagnosis. This result is in accordance with studies from the economic field, suggesting that unemployment is an important risk factor for future unemployment. It might be that the worsening of health may be accelerated by the stress and psychological and socio-economic disadvantages of unemployment, and that marginalization in the labor market may be accelerated by health-related factors. Thus, unemployment before diagnosis should be considered in future studies of BCS. Introduction Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma of Bone (UPSB), formerly named Malignant Fibrous Histiocytoma of Bone (MFHB), represents a rare intraosseous malignancy. Morphologically, this tumor closely resembles osteosarcoma but lacks osteoid formation. UPSB must be distinguished from Undifferentiated Pleomorphic Sarcoma of the Soft Tissues, the latter being one of the more frequent soft-tissue sarcomas of the adult population and treated accordingly (WHO Classification of Tumours ). If left without systemic therapy, UPSB, like osteosarcoma, carries a considerable risk of metastatic spread. Based upon histologic and clinical similarities to this more common malignancy of bone, it is usually treated according to principles established there (Strauss et al. ; Pediatric Treatment Editorial and Board ). Surgery and multi-agent chemotherapy represent the mainstay of treatment. The background upon which decision making is based on is, however, limited. Only few series have gathered more than fifty affected patients. These were generally retrospective (Capanna et al. ; Nishida et al. ; Bielack et al. ; Nagano et al. ; Boudou-Rouquette et al. ; Gusho et al. ). UPSB was the focus of only very few prospective series in highly selected groups of patients (Bramwell et al. ; Palmerini et al. ). We set out to further clinically delineate this tumor and its prognosis. The Cooperative Osteosarcoma Study Group’s (COSS) database offered a unique opportunity to do so. The large, multi-centric COSS-group covers the three German speaking countries of Europe. It has been registering UPSB alongside osteosarcoma from its advent over 45 years ago. It was always recommended to treat UPSB according to the same principles as osteosarcoma. This paper now reports upon the group’s experience with this rare osseous malignancy. Patients and methods Patient selection and data collection COSS includes centers from Germany, Austria, and Switzerland and registers patients with osteosarcomas and related malignancies. Its database was now searched for patients with UPSB diagnosed 1980–2020. They were included into this analysis unless their follow-up was < 100 days without having suffered an event. Patients were followed until 2021 or the date of last available information, respectively. All COSS-study and -registry protocols were performed in accordance with the Code of Ethics of the World Medical Association (Declaration of Helsinki) and approved by the appropriate ethics committee (Ethik-Kommission bei der Ärztekammer Hamburg nos. 500, 1147; Ethikkommission der Ärztekammer Westfalen-Lippe und der Westfälischen-Wilhelms Universität nos. 182/98 Biel2, 4IV Bie 2, 4 I Bielack, 5 V. Bielack; and Ethik-Kommission an der Medizinischen Fakultät der Eberhard-Karls-Universität und am Universitätsklinikum Tübingen no. 5 V Bielack). Informed consent was required from all patients and/or their legal guardians, whichever appropriate. COSS-recruitment policies as well as the treatment of enrolled patients, which include those with UPSB, have been described in detail (Bielack et al. , ; Ferrari et al. ; Smeland et al. ). Demographic and therapy data were collected prospectively. Additional information was collected retrospectively from available status report forms, radiology, pathology, and surgery reports, as well as progress letters. All patient-charts at the central COSS-office were screened for additional relevant information by the first author. The diagnosis of UPSB required histologic verification, preferentially with reference-pathology. Local and systemic staging procedures were performed according to standards defined for osteosarcoma. These included investigations of the primary tumor, the lung, and distant bones. X-rays of the primary and the lungs as well as bone-scintigraphy were always prescribed. The use of other investigations (computed tomography and/or magnetic resonance imaging and/or positron emission tomography) varied with time and availability. Systemic treatment of UPSB, including pre- and postoperative chemotherapy, followed the guidelines and guidance developed for osteosarcoma. Drugs administered almost always included doxorubicin, high-dose methotrexate (with limitations according to age in patients over 40 years), and cisplatin. Ifosfamide was prescribed in a considerable number of regimens. Other agents were rarely part of the protocols. Local therapy was by complete surgical removal of the primary as well as any primary metastases, if present. The goal of surgical therapy was to achieve wide surgical margins (Enneking et al. ). The histologic response of the primary to pre-operative chemotherapy was graded according to Salzer-Kuntschik et al ( ). Radiotherapy was not part of any COSS-regimen but to be considered in inoperable situations. The COSS-office together with panels of experts was available for guidance in case of questions regarding local or systemic therapies or treatment-complications. The date of diagnostic biopsy was used as the starting date for all survival-analyses. Follow-up was until last available information or death, whichever appropriate. Event-free survival was calculated until the date of recurrence, date of last contact, or date of death, whichever first, overall-survival until death or last contact, respectively. Patients not having achieved a macroscopically complete remission considering all sites of disease were assumed to have suffered an event on day 1. The sites involved by first recurrences were coded. To our knowledge, it represents one of the largest cohorts of such tumors studied so far. As systemic therapy has changed only little over the years, the ensuing findings may be used as a benchmark. The analysis does not come without limitations. For one, it is unknown which proportion of patients with UPSB cared for in contributing centers was indeed registered. As a result, it cannot be claimed that this report is truly population based. Some variables had to be investigated using somewhat incomplete datasets. However, sufficient data was available to allow analyzing even those. Of note, all patients received a recommendation for combined modality therapy. Therefore, no information on patients treated by local approaches only is available. Hence, no internal comparison to such patients is feasible. Osteosarcoma, on the other hand, may show detectable predispositions in around a quarter of cases (Mirabello et al. ). The early time-period in which some of the UPSB studied were detected makes their molecular testing unlikely. Additionally, not all positive genetic findings may have been reported. Still, the observation is of potential interest, particularly as other reports offer little information regarding this topic at all. UPSB must certainly be included among tumors which may be caused by radiation. The age at which UPSB was diagnosed in this series, a median of over 40 years, clearly distinguishes this tumor from osteosarcoma. Data from the SEER-registry point to a similar median age (Gusho et al. ). Osteosarcoma, particularly if located in an extremity, is strongly related to the age of maximal bone growth, adolescence. The factor of bone-growth is clearly less pronounced in UPSB. As a consequence, it is less the pediatrician but rather the medical oncologist who will face affected patients. Other than the distribution of ages, that of genders seems to reflect that of osteosarcoma (Beird et al. ), males more likely affected. Again similar to osteosarcoma (Beird et al. ), UPSB shares a predilection for the extremities and, there, the knee, where almost three quarters of extremity UPSB were located. Some ten percent of cases affected the axial skeleton and isolated cases even craniofacial sites. It seems that any region of the body may be affected. UPSB size at detection seems somewhat smaller than in osteosarcoma. It exceeded one third of the involved bone in less than one fifth of cases, compared to one third in the latter (Bielack et al. ). Despite the often limited size, however, UPSB frequently led to pathologic fractures, these affecting approximately one out of seven patients. The purely osteolytic nature is probably predisposing. Pathologic fracture usually occurred prior to tumor-diagnosis, making a high index of suspicion advisable. Primary metastases were fairly uncommon. Those few detected favored the same sites as these do in osteosarcoma, namely the lungs and, less often, distant bones. Owing to the evolution of diagnostic techniques, some cases might have escaped detection in the earlier years covered by this study. Still, UPSB appears less likely to spread primarily than osteosarcoma. Not surprising for a multi-center group focusing on chemotherapy, all patients in this series received systemic treatment. Regimens designed against osteosarcoma were administered (Bielack et al. ). That only two thirds of UPSB-patients received pre-operative chemotherapy may be best explained by their relatively advanced age. Older individuals are known to frequently proceed straight to surgery (Ferrari et al. ) (Bielack et al. ). After treatment, more than 90% of the UPSB in this series went into complete remission. With a median follow-up period of more than five years, outcome-results may be considered sufficiently mature. Both the types of secondary malignancies occurring during this time-period and their incidence seem quite typical for what our group observed in heavily treated bone-sarcoma patients (Kube et al. ). The event-free survival probability, almost two thirds at five years, seems remarkable, as patients were mostly of a rather advanced age. Here, UPSB seems to behave more positively than does osteosarcoma. If secondary metastases occurred, these generally affected the lungs and distant bones, just like osteosarcoma (Beird et al. ). A few individuals, however, developed recurrences at sites quite unusual for the latter tumor. As expected, given the moderate rate of recurrences, approximately two thirds of patients survived for at least five years. Most deaths observed were directly attributable to UPSB. Some therapy related causes, secondary malignancies, unrelated causes, and unknown causes also contributed. Several potentially relevant prognostic could be dereced. Some were expected: Patients aged less than 40 years did better than older ones. Patients with extremity primaries did better than those with tumors located elsewhere. Patients whose disease had already spread at diagnosis did worse than those with localized tumors. There were only very few affected patients in this series but their prognosis was grim. Pathologic fractures were associated with an inferior outcome. In this context, it is interesting to note that such is also found for older—but not younger—osteosarcoma patients (Kelley et al. ). The reasons for ablative surgery producing better results than limb-salvage are certainly complex. Any interpretation is certainly not straightforward. Far less surprisingly, patients who failed to achieve a complete remission generally also failed to survive. It may be interesting to take a closer look at some factors not found significant. Here, reference pathology, symptom duration, and patient gender seemed of minor impact. Remarkably, initial tumor-size did not seem predictive. This is in clear distinction to osteosarcoma (Bielack et al. ). Maybe even more strikingly, we could observe no significant correlation between tumor-response and prognosis, poor responders doing just as well as good responders. In osteosarcoma, on the other hand, response is one of the most important predictors of prognosis (Beird et al. ; Bielack et al. ). It seems that a poor response of an UPSB must not be a cause of unnecessary concern. The UPSB described in this series were treated on regimens designed against osteosarcoma and not on protocols against soft-tissue sarcoma. In the latter tumors, cisplatin and methotrexate have not been proven particularly efficacious. Anthracyclines and ifosfamide, however, have very much been so. If choosing chemotherapy against UPSB, it remains open whether regimens absolutely identical to those designed against osteosarcoma represent the optimal choice. Still, in the absence of superior alternatives, these may currently represent valid options. In summary, this series describes four decades of multi-institutional experience with UPSB treated in the German-speaking region of Europe. It depicts many clinical similarities of UPSB to osteosarcoma but also delineates some important differences. Maybe most notably, an inferior local response to chemotherapy in no way predicts systemic failures. Given the results achieved, it seems reasonable to continue choosing osteosarcoma-regimens if planning to employ chemotherapy against UPSB.

Introduction Several chronic diseases, such as rheumatic, endocrinologic, and neoplastic diseases, have seen a transformation in the available treatment options, moving towards the utilization of disease-modifying agents and targeted biologic therapies capable of decelerating or halting disease progression. Concurrently, the treatment objectives have evolved to prioritize the induction of sustained disease remission or, when remission is not achievable, the maintenance of sustained minimal disease activity. A similar trend has emerged in chronic allergic diseases. Recent advances in immunobiological and other targeted therapies have shifted the therapeutic paradigm in allergy and clinical immunology care from control to the possibility of achieving clinical remission. However, despite the expanding body of evidence across multiple immune-mediated diseases traditionally managed within Allergy and Clinical Immunology, the field still lacks a standardized and validated framework for defining clinical remission, establishing measurable endpoints, and enabling cross-disease comparisons. Definition of remission in immunoallergic diseases Currently, there is no universal definition of “remission”. A comprehensive and pragmatic definition of remission, whether based on clinical evolution or as a treatment target, must add value beyond the existing treatments for the control of immune-mediated diseases. This is particularly important in asthma, where current symptom control and future risk of adverse outcomes are key considerations. Although there are clear criteria for optimal control of a patient's symptoms over the past 4 weeks, we lack explicit goals for disease control over longer time intervals. During recent decades, the introduction of biologic therapies and other treatments (eg, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors for atopic dermatitis) have transformed the management of chronic allergic diseases, marking a paradigm shift from merely controlling symptoms to the potential of achieving long-term remission. Initially used to reduce the frequency of exacerbations, and improve disease control, biologics now target specific immunological pathways, offering personalised and effective treatment, leading to significant improvements in patient outcomes. With fewer side effects and reduced need for systemic corticosteroids, patients benefit from improved disease control and enhanced quality of life. Ultimately, the future of allergy treatment lies in early intervention, biomarker-driven strategies, and expanding indications, aiming for sustained remission, and even potential modification of the natural history of the disease. Clinical remission (CR) refers to a sustained state of complete absence of clinically relevant disease manifestations, including symptoms, exacerbations, and functional deterioration, over a defined period of time. CR is defined independently of underlying biological activity. Suppression of inflammatory pathways and normalization of biomarkers define biological remission, which may coexist with, but is not required for, clinical remission. , While it does not necessarily imply a cure, it reflects an optimal and sustained clinical outcome, with minimal clinical burden and reduced risk of future disease progression. Types of remission Spontaneous remission refers to the natural course of the disease. It occurs independently of medical intervention (eg, in chronic spontaneous urticaria, the disease resolves spontaneously in 40%–80% of patients within the first 5 years, regardless of the pharmacotherapy used). Clinical remission can be defined by the absence of significant symptoms and signs (eg, no asthma exacerbations or pruritus in atopic dermatitis), stability of objective disease parameters relevant to the affected organ system (such as lung function in asthma), and sustained disease inactivity over time. - Clinical remission on treatment refers to remission achieved while the patient is still receiving pharmacologic therapy, excluding systemic corticosteroids, which are not considered acceptable maintenance therapy in this context. - Clinical remission off treatment is characterized by the absence of symptoms and disease activity without any ongoing pharmacological treatment (except for supportive non-pharmacological measures, if applicable). Biological remission refers to normalization of inflammatory biomarkers (eg, eosinophils, IgE, FeNO) and reduced tissue inflammation confirmed through specific diagnostic tests. Considering the emerging evidence that biologic therapies may also influence structural airway changes, including elements of airway remodeling, this component could eventually be incorporated as an additional criterion of biological remission in asthma. Functional remission can translate to the restoration of normal organ function, which must also be considered as part of asthma, where at least stability or improvement in lung function is already a criterion to be fulfilled. Mechanisms and influencing factors for remission Remission in allergic diseases is becoming an increasingly attainable goal, driven by more profound insights into immunological mechanisms and the development of targeted therapies. A key factor is immune regulation, involving a shift from a type 2 (T2) inflammatory profile, dominated by TH2 and ILC2 cells, towards a more tolerogenic and less reactive immune state characterized by attenuation of type 2 cytokine signalling, enhanced regulatory pathways, and decreased effector cell activation. This immunological reprogramming includes induction of regulatory T cells, suppression of IgE-mediated pathways with downregulation of FcεRI expression, reduced activation of mast cells and eosinophils, and modulation of epithelial–immune crosstalk, including inhibition of alarmins such as TSLP and IL-33. The use of targeted biologics, such as omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, dupilumab, and tezepelumab, which block IgE and critical mediators like IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and TLSP, has enabled not only effective disease control but also sustained CR in many patients. Early intervention, biomarker-guided patient selection, environmental control, and treatment of relevant comorbidities may critically influence the probability, depth, and durability of remission. , Furthermore, allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT) with aeroallergens or with food allergens, together with allergen exposure reduction, plays a key role in modulating the immune response and sustaining, at least, CR. , Clinical relevance of remission Clinical remission represents a higher-order therapeutic goal that goes beyond traditional concepts of disease control or response. While clinical control focuses on short-term symptom suppression, remission aims at sustained disease quiescence and, potentially, normalization of the disease trajectory and long-term prognosis. In this context, remission should be interpreted as a state of minimal disease burden over time, rather than merely optimal short-term control. Clinical remission in asthma Although CR in asthma was first considered in 1951 with spontaneous remission being higher in childhood, a new concrete interest in CR, as a multicriteria tool to evaluate treatment response in asthma, increased rapidly in the last 5 years. Importantly, CR in asthma should be interpreted within the conceptual framework of asthma control, which integrates both current symptom control and future risk domains. Accordingly, remission encompasses not only the absence of symptoms, but also sustained protection against severe exacerbations, stability or improvement of lung function, and minimization of systemic corticosteroid exposure over time. A definition of CR in asthma was presented in the 2020 Expert Consensus Framework for Asthma Remission as a Treatment Goal. It included the following criteria: 1.) no apparent asthma symptoms, 2.) optimized and stabilized pulmonary function, 3.) patient and health care provider agreement regarding presence of disease remission, and 4.) no systemic corticosteroid therapy for exacerbation treatment or long-term management. The “need” to adopt such a tool has been highlighted, , mainly as the use of biologics in severe asthma has increasingly prompted researchers and clinicians to define better and recognize their clinical impact. Several definitions of CR have been published thereafter. We herein report the most used criteria defining CR: no apparent asthma symptoms, no exacerbation, no oral corticosteroid (OCS) use for exacerbation treatment or long-term management, and stable lung function for 12 months. , , Spontaneous remission has been reported in children, with approximately 20% achieving normalization of airway hyperresponsiveness as well; this phenomenon has not been reported in adults. More studies are needed to define each subset population able to reach CR with each biologic. However, the overall success with biologics in clinical trials, ranging between 36 and 42% is modest, and is even less impressive in real life registries such as the International Severe Asthma Registry (ISAR). These remission rates likely reflect multiple determinants. Although highly effective therapies targeting type-2 inflammatory pathways are available, a ceiling effect in treatment response probably exists. These remission rates likely reflect multiple determinants. Although highly effective therapies targeting type-2 inflammatory pathways are available, a ceiling effect in treatment response probably exists. Structural airway changes, persistent airway hyperresponsiveness, non-T2 inflammatory mechanisms, and the impact of comorbidities may limit the proportion of patients who can achieve complete remission even with optimized biologic therapy. Using airway biomarkers in sputum and a comprehensive airway-inflammometry-guided strategy, the McMaster University group in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada reported remission rates of 61–67% in selected severe asthma cohorts. However, these estimates depend on the specific remission criteria applied and therefore are not directly comparable with more stringent definitions of clinical remission proposed in other frameworks. The residual symptoms were driven by immunodeficiencies leading to airway infections, moderate to severe airway hyperresponsiveness indicating airway smooth muscle reactivity, and airway mucus that was possibly associated with non-T2 processes. An additional dimension of asthma remission that must be considered is its durability over time. Emerging longitudinal data indicate that remission may not be a permanent state in a subset of patients. Approximately 30% of individuals who initially achieve clinical remission may subsequently experience relapse, which suggests that remission should be interpreted as a dynamic state rather than a definitive cure. Understanding the mechanisms underlying loss of remission, including persistent airway remodeling, comorbidities, environmental exposures, or incomplete suppression of inflammatory pathways, will be essential for guiding long-term treatment strategies and follow-up. Very recent data from SA registries , have demonstrated that inhaled treatment alone may be sufficient to achieve CR in a subset of patients. All these data clearly underpin the need to more properly define the eligibility of SA patients for each treatment, using Precision Medicine. Unfortunately, there is no international consensus on the Clinical Remission Definition, although a call to action has been recently proposed. CR has been assessed primarily in patients with severe asthma using biologic agents; but this concept may also be relevant for patients with milder to moderate asthma, where CR may be more easily obtainable in cases with no significant airway impairment. In summary, there is a need to define complete remission, where other criteria such as anti-inflammatory effects and/or regression of airway remodeling will hopefully be included. Achieving this goal is not “cookie cutter medicine”. This needs the development of point of care airway biomarkers and multiscale integration of various “omics platforms” to get handprints of endotypes of the individual patient's pathobiology to truly individualize treatment. Clinical remission in allergic rhinitis Remission in allergic rhinitis (AR) has been reported in epidemiological studies to occur in 25%–32% of patients. The associated factors have been diverse and controversial, like the presence or absence of asthma symptoms, environmental conditions, age and gender. In these studies, clinical remission was defined as the absence of AR symptoms in the most recent follow-up evaluations. Remission in AR, as in asthma, was also reported to occur as a result of allergen immunotherapy (AIT) intervention, including in the remission group those patients without the need of antihistamines and/or intranasal corticosteroids by the time the study outcomes were measured, on average 4.5 years of AIT. , In a non-interventional, long-term follow-up of over a thousand children from 4 to 24 years old, it was speculated that the small percentage of remission in 21.5% resulted from a dynamic spontaneous tolerance from 16 to 24 years old, correlated with the loss of sensitization. Although no standardized definition of remission was reported, individuals with pollen sensitization, who no longer presented with AR symptoms, were classified as being in remission. Allergen-specific IgE sensitization levels may also valuable tool to predict, in some patients, the possibility of achieving remission. Nevertheless, no biomarkers currently demonstrate high accuracy in predicting the clinical response. In addition to the disease burden and the decline in quality of life caused by AR, there are also significant associated costs that could be considered as a parameter in defining AR remission. In summary, no clear AR remission has been reported, and the term usually considered has been applied to a patient who remains symptom-free at follow-up (regardless of the time of year), with a history of only occasional medication use at the time of their evaluation. Clinical remission in chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps The natural course of nasal polyposis and T2 inflammation, unfortunately, features nasal polyps (NP) with frequent recurrence following either oral corticosteroid therapy, with or without antibiotics, or surgical intervention. Although endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) does not cure T2 inflammation, it is a widely accepted modality for CRSwNP management. The natural course of CRS without polyps is less known. The ESS reboot technique is reportedly associated with a lower cumulative recurrence rate of NP (8%) than non-reboot techniques (45%) at 3 years postoperatively. , Following surgery, the recurrence rate can range from 3.5% at 12 months from index surgery, to 79% at a 12 years observation period postoperatively. , , , Risk factors for NP recurrence can include smoking, presence of asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), or prior ESS, in addition to markers of eosinophilic inflammation. These can include tissue eosinophilia or eosinophilic aggregates in the mucin suctioned during surgery. , , , , Revision surgery for NP carries a risk for recurrence ranging from 14% to 24% over 90 months. Pharmacotherapy of recurrent NP is multifaceted. Doubling the dose of nasal corticosteroid spray following primary surgery can be safe and more efficacious than single doses. Also, corticosteroid irrigation following surgery can be superior to nasal steroid spray. Topical antibiotics have been described sporadically in recurrent NP, yet no clear evidence for their efficacy exists. NP recurrence following primary surgery can be an indication for biological therapy. When carefully selected, patients who fail ESS can improve significantly on monoclonal antibody therapy, most notably dupilumab and tezepelumab. , In summary, CR in CRSwNP can be defined as a prolonged state (≥12 months) without bothersome symptoms and signs (eg, rhinorrhea, anosmia and nasal obstruction, as possible evaluated by objective measures), no requirement for systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics and endoscopic revision surgery, no impact on quality of life, and endoscopic resolution of nasal polyps. , Clinical remission in chronic urticaria The World Allergy Organisation (WAO) Urticaria Committee systematically reviewed available studies focusing on chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) that included at least a one-year follow-up. The available information was limited, and therefore it was not possible to determine the optimal time point to define CSU remission. However, nearly all groups that conducted longitudinal studies assessing the frequency of remission agreed to use this term when patients remained free of urticaria signs and symptoms for 6–12 months without any treatment, including antihistamines, omalizumab, cyclosporine, or corticosteroids. , , , , , So far, no evidence exists to propose any biomarkers for defining inflammatory or mechanistic remission in CSU or identifying patients with “cure”. In summary, based on the systematic review and the consensus reached by a panel of experts grounded in the current available literature, clinical remission in CSU was defined as the complete resolution of urticaria signs and symptoms without the use of pharmacotherapy for at least 6 months. The implications of this definition in clinical practice must be evaluated and validated in future studies. Currently, there is no global consensus on the definition of remission in chronic inducible urticaria. Clinical remission in mastocytosis Mastocytosis encompasses a spectrum of clonal mast cell disorders with distinct endotypes and phenotypes, including cutaneous and systemic forms, the latter classified as indolent, smoldering, and advanced. The onset and natural history of cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) differ significantly from systemic mastocytosis (SM). Childhood-onset CM is generally considered a benign condition with a high likelihood of spontaneous remission around puberty, whereas SM typically develops later in life and persists chronically. , , Treatment of CM is primarily symptomatic and preventive, usually without the need for cytoreductive medications, as spontaneous remission is common, particularly in pediatric cases. In this context, spontaneous remission refers to the natural resolution of skin lesions and mast cell-related symptoms without medical intervention and, in some cases, may be clinically indistinguishable from cure, although long-term follow-up remains essential. , CM begins before the first year of life in the majority of pediatric cases, and long-term observational studies report significant or complete remission of skin lesions and symptoms in approximately half after 10 years of follow-up, with partial remission observed in additional 30% of cases. , Longer follow-up studies have reported complete remission rates of approximately two-thirds of pediatric cases, although diffuse CM may regress more slowly and occasionally persist into adulthood. , Systemic mastocytosis is currently not considered a curable disease. Patients with indolent SM experience significant morbidity, including an increased risk of anaphylaxis, but overall life expectancy is similar to that of the general

Patients with indolent SM experience significant morbidity, including an increased risk of anaphylaxis, but overall life expectancy is similar to that of the general population. , , In contrast, advanced SM is associated with high mortality, and progressive disease, including aggressive mastocytosis, SM with associated hematologic malignancies, and mast cell leukemia. , Until recently, the management of SM focused mainly on symptom control. However, with the advent of more effective and safer cytoreductive therapies, clinical trials have begun to establish criteria for both partial and major responses, as well as for partial and complete remissions. Cytoreductive therapies have also started to be used in some cases of indolent SM, particularly in patients with a high burden of symptoms or impaired quality of life despite optimal symptomatic treatment. , , Partial remission in SM has been defined by significant clinical improvement accompanied by a substantial reduction in mast cell burden and disease markers, particularly tryptase, without full normalization. Complete remission requires disappearance of disease-related signs and symptoms, normalization of serum tryptase levels, resolution of organ involvement, and absence of detectable neoplastic mast cells in bone marrow or other tissues. , , Quantification of KIT D816V mutant allele burden in peripheral blood has emerged as a valuable biomarker correlating with disease activity and response to therapy and is increasingly incorporated into remission assessment. In summary, clinical remission in mastocytosis should primarily be defined by sustained absence of clinically relevant symptoms and disease activity over time. Biological markers, including serum tryptase levels and KIT D816V allele burden, should be considered supportive indicators of biological remission rather than mandatory criteria for defining clinical remission. Clinical remission in atopic dermatitis Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disorder and is recognized as the most prevalent form of chronic inflammatory dermatosis. , , Spontaneous remission has been described in a large proportion of the pediatric population and, less frequently, in adults. Diagnosis is primarily guided by clinical criteria. Numerous scales are utilized to assess the severity of AD, including the Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) index, the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) and the Investigator Global Assessment (IGA). , Appropriate management for this condition involves a multifaceted approach that incorporates avoidance of irritants and allergens (if sensitized), emollients, topical corticosteroids (TCS), calcineurin inhibitors (TCI) (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus), topical PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole, roflumilast), topical JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib, delgocitinib, aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist tapinarof, among others. For moderate to severe cases of AD, treatment may escalate to include systemic immunomodulators, monoclonal antibodies, such as the IL-4/IL-13 inhibitor dupilumab, IL-13 inhibitors tralokinumab and lebrikizumab, IL-31 inhibitor nemolizumab, and JAK inhibitors, such as baricitinib, abrocitinib, and upadacitinib, all aimed at achieving clinical remission of atopic dermatitis. , , , , , , , , , , The absence of standardized definitions for remission in chronic diseases leads to inconsistencies in therapeutic outcomes and long-term monitoring. Remission can be classified as partial (disease severity is minimal and does not significantly impact the patient's daily life but there is still evidence for residual biological activity) or complete (Eczema Area Severity Index = 0, SCORAD <10, Validated IGA score = 0, DLQI = 0; Pruritus Score = 0); and can be temporary (<12 months with no exacerbation) or long term (>12 months with no exacerbation), and can be achieved with or with no pharmacologic therapy (excluding the use of systemic corticosteroids). In summary, for atopic dermatitis, since there is no objective parameter or biologic marker to use (except maybe skin biopsy which is not recommended routinely), we propose defining clinical remission as complete symptom resolution for at least 12 months without exacerbations and minimal or no treatment (but considering the use of emollients). Establishing such evidence will support the development and broader acceptance of consensus definitions for remission in atopic dermatitis. While we do not have any agreed-upon definition of remission in FA, a recent authoritative study proposed to consider FA outgrown when the above mentioned 3 patient-related components are realized. When remission is not spontaneous, none of the current FA treatments can achieve it. Desensitization, the classical outcome of oral immunotherapy and omalizumab, identifies an increased threshold allergen dose for clinical reactions after food ingestion. In interventional FA studies, the efficacy of treatments is generally measured based on desensitization, assuming that an increased threshold provides patient protection from allergic reactions after accidently ingesting the allergen. If so, they are expected to experience less severe and/or less frequent allergic reactions. , A persistent increase in allergen threshold, indicated with the term “sustained unresponsiveness” (SU), is another accepted outcome. In summary, younger children (<3 years of age), especially those with lower IgE levels at diagnosis, tend to have better chances of achieving remission. In this age range, it has been suggested that a window of opportunity exists to foster remission following AIT. This has been explored in studies with oral, epicutaneous, and sublingual AIT in young children. Further studies, with long-term follow-up, are expected to validate this hypothesis. Clinical remission in eosinophilic esophagitis Remission in eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) patients is described in the literature according to 3 main definitions: histological remission, clinical or symptomatic remission, and complete remission, the last including both histological and symptomatic components. , , Histological remission relies on intraepithelial peak eosinophil count (PEC). Despite some variability related to the cut-offs reported by different studies, most of the randomized clinical trials defined remission in terms of a PEC of between 0 and ≤5 per HPF (high-power field). , Of note, restricting remission assessment on the PEC only might lead to neglecting other specific histological features related to active disease even in the presence of low eosinophil counts. Eosinophilic Esophagitis Histology Scoring System (EoEHSS) can capture eosinophilic micro-abscesses, basal cell hyperplasia, or extracellular eosinophil granules, and a REoEHSS score of ≤3 has been suggested as a further remission criterion to be combined with PEC. Clinical or symptomatic remission can be assessed through different tools: a) the eosinophilic Esophagitis Activity Index (EEsAI), whose score for a non-active disease is ≤ 20; b) the dysphagia and odynophagia severity score, if ≤ 2 suggesting disease remission; and c) Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire (DSQ) score which defines EoE remission in the case of a >90% reduction compared to baseline. , In summary, complete remission was defined as the combination of low symptoms and low eosinophil infiltration in biopsy samples. Of note, low correlation between symptoms and endoscopic or histological features , is a quite common occurrence in EoE patients. Combining EoEHSS and EEsAI is currently recommended for an accurate disease remission assessment. , Remission as a unifying outcome: a World Allergy Organization (WAO) framework proposal Several chronic conditions (eg, rheumatoid arthritis) have successfully adopted remission as a treatment goal. Allergic diseases have also demonstrated that long-term remission is achievable, namely through pharmacological, biological, small molecule and allergen-specific immunotherapy. However, definitions of remission across the spectrum of allergic diseases remain heterogeneous and no universally accepted remission criteria exist, partly because clinical trials have focused on disease control as an outcome, and there is a lack of validated tools for comparing treatment outcomes across diseases. , In general, CR will be a sustained state (eg, 6 or 12 months) of absent significant clinical symptoms, low or normalized inflammatory activity, and preserved or improved organ function, achieved with (Clinical Remission on Treatment – CRt) or without ongoing targeted therapy, and without the use of systemic corticosteroids or rescue medications ( ). Once clinical remission is achieved, whether with (CRt) or without treatment (CR), it does not imply disease cure but rather a sustained state of disease inactivity with minimal burden. In this context, shared decision-making becomes essential to guide individualized step-down strategies. , Clinicians should engage patients in discussions regarding the potential to taper or discontinue maintenance therapies, particularly systemic medications, while closely monitoring for early signs of relapse. This lack of harmonization limits cross-disease comparison, interpretation of long-term outcomes, and translation of precision medicine into clinical practice, supporting the need for a coordinated global WAO initiative to define and implement a transversal concept of clinical remission in different immunoallergic diseases, supported by a modular, simple and effective disease-adaptable scoring tool (the Allergic Disease Remission Score - ADReS) ( , and ) as a step toward standardizing modern treatment outcomes in allergic diseases. Within the 3D-CR framework, the clinical domain represents the core requirement for remission. Biological or functional improvement in the absence of clinical stability, such as persistent need for maintenance oral corticosteroids, should not be interpreted as remission. The 3D-CR framework is intended as a conceptual and research framework to characterize remission states across diseases and facilitate harmonization of outcomes in clinical trials and registries. It is not designed as a prescriptive algorithm mandating therapeutic escalation in clinically well-controlled patients. A patient in clinical remission with residual biomarker abnormalities may represent an optimal therapeutic response rather than treatment failure. The ADReS score is intended primarily as a research and monitoring tool to facilitate standardized assessment of remission across diseases rather than a rigid therapeutic decision algorithm. Establishing such a framework is essential not only for harmonizing clinical research but also for guiding long-term treatment strategies in the era of precision medicine. Future research should focus on validating remission frameworks, identifying reliable biomarkers of disease inactivity, and integrating remission endpoints into clinical trials and registries. chunks.content: Introduction Hepatoblastoma (HB) is the most common malignant liver tumor of childhood. , Children with metastatic disease at diagnosis fare poorly, with event-free survival (EFS) of 20-50% in the majority of reported series. - HB patients who have low alpha fetoprotein (AFP) levels at diagnosis (< 100 ng/ml) have had poor outcomes in the past. However, modern pathology has suggested that these low AFP tumors were more likely to have been malignant rhabdoid tumors of the liver. , Chemotherapy is an essential part of treatment for this high-risk patient group. The mainstay of most chemotherapy regimens has been cisplatin and doxorubicin which are dose-limited due to renal, auditory, and cardiac toxicities. - Other agents such as carboplatin, ifosfamide, and etoposide have also been used in various combinations with minimal improvement in EFS. , Because of the rarity of HB, traditional phase I and phase II clinical trial mechanisms have generally been unsuccessful in identifying novel effective agents. The SIOPEL (International Childhood Liver Tumors Strategy Group) group demonstrated improved survival in high-risk patients using dose-dense cisplatin and doxorubicin in SIOPEL-4, a promising pilot study. Still, the significant toxicities associated with these two agents limit the total dose that can be administered during treatment and are associated with significant morbidity in patients who are cured of their disease. Therefore, there is still a significant need to identify novel agents that can improve the suboptimal outcomes and minimize late effects for these high-risk patients. The initial vincristine/irinotecan (VI) high-risk stratum of AHEP0731 was selected based on data from phase I and phase II pediatric solid tumor trials, in which several patients with HB had good responses to therapy. - Additionally, significant anecdotal evidence demonstrated the efficacy of VI and single agent irinotecan in refractory and relapsed HB. - A SIOPEL trial using single agent irinotecan dosed daily for 5 days in consecutive weeks also had partial responses using AFP and Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria in 6 of 24 relapsed or refractory patients. The rationale for adding temsirolimus to the VI backbone was multi-faceted. Temsirolimus is an inhibitor of mTOR (the mammalian target of rapamycin), a component of the TORC1 complex that senses the nutritional status of cells (e.g., amino acids, oxygen tension, glucose, and in mammalian cells, growth factor signaling), , and regulates cell cycle entry from G1 into S phase. mTOR also regulates protein synthesis of HIF (hypoxia inducible factors) proteins. - These proteins regulate tumor angiogenesis and survival pathways that permit tumor growth in the hypoxic conditions common in many solid tumors. Preclinical cancer models suggested that an mTOR inhibitor in combination with irinotecan would have at least additive anti-tumor effect although such preclinical work did not spefically include testing of temsirolimus against HB cell lines or patient samples. Additionally, the systemic toxicity of temsirolimus does not overlap with the adverse effects seen with irinotecan or vincristine. Finally, since mTOR inhibitors are used to prevent solid organ rejection, mTOR inhibitor use in children with high-risk hepatoblastoma, some of whom may need liver transplantation, might have a dual benefit in concurrently providing graft rejection prophylaxis and treating minimal residual disease. Dosing for temsirolimus was based on the Children’s Oncology Group study ADVL0918, a phase I trial of temsirolimus in combination with irinotecan and temozolomide. The optimal method for assessing response to novel agents is controversial. RECIST criteria are typically used but have significant limitations. Furthermore, radiographic response does not necessarily correlate with cellular events within the tumor. Identification of biologic markers may be more reliable in assessing the efficacy of a novel agent or combination. Serum AFP is an excellent biomarker for HB response to treatment because decline of AFP has been shown to be prognsotic. Both radiographic and AFP criteria should be used to assess response to therapy in HB. The Children’s Oncology Group (COG) Study for the Treatment of Children with All Stages of Hepatoblastoma, AHEP0731, included strata for high-risk patients that would explore innovative agents. Two cycles of vincristine, irinotecan, and temsirolimus (VIT) were administered in an upfront window for patients with high-risk metastatic HB. We report the response rate of two cycles of VIT in newly diagnosed children with high-risk HB as well as their overall outcomes and compare that to the response rate and outcomes of a previously studied vincristine/irinotecan arm. Methods Study Patients: Patients with newly diagnosed, previously untreated biopsy-proven HB were eligible for high-risk window chemotherapy if they had either metastatic disease or a serum AFP level of < 100 ng/ml at diagnosis, irrespective of stage. The National Cancer Institute, the Pediatric Central IRB, and the institutional review boards of the participating institutions approved the protocol. Informed consent was obtained for all patients prior to treatment according to Department of Health and Human Services guidelines. Staging: Patients were staged for risk classification using COG staging guidelines prior to the initiation of chemotherapy: stage I, complete gross resection with clear margins; stage II, gross total resection with microscopic residual disease at the margins of resection or preoperative/intra-operative tumor rupture; stage III, gross total resection with nodal involvement or incomplete resection with gross residual intrahepatic disease; stage IV, metastatic disease with either complete or incomplete resection. PRETEXT (pretreatment extent of disease) grouping was also to be done for all patients at diagnosis and at any time when subsequent abdominal scans were performed preoperatively called POSTTEXT (posttreatment extent of disease if assigned after chemotherapy) ( ). PRETEXT grouping was not to be used for risk classification but was to guide the surgical approach, specifically to help determine which patients should be considered to have resectable/unresectable tumors at diagnosis. All diagnostic and follow up imaging was centrally reviewed for response assessment. Central determination of PRETEXT and POSTTEXT was based on the consensus of the study panel of two radiologists and up to 6 surgeons. Chemotherapy: Patients received vincristine (V) 1.5 mg/m 2 /dose (0.05 mg/kg/dose for patients < 10 kg) intravenously on days 1 and 8, in combination with irinotecan (I) 50 mg/m 2 /dose (1.67 mg/kg/dose for patients < 10 kg) intravenously days 1-5, and temsirolimus (T) 35 mg/m 2 /dose (1.2 mg/kg/dose for patients < 10 kg) intravenously on days 1 and 8 ( ). A second cycle of VIT was repeated after 21 days if safety criteria were met. Criteria included: 1) ANC ≥ 750/μL, 2) platelet count ≥ 75,000/μL, 3) total cholesterol ≤ 400 mg/dL OR ≤ 500 mg/dL and on lipid lowering medication, and 4) triglycerides ≤ 300 mg/dL OR ≤ 500 mg/dL and on lipid lowering medication. Repeat imaging and AFP measurements were performed after 2 cycles of the upfront window therapy and all patients were centrally reviewed for response to VIT. Patients who were considered responders according to local assessment received 2 additional cycles of VIT intermixed with 6 cycles of (C5VD) which consisted of cisplatin (100 mg/m 2 /dose or 3.3 mg/kg/dose for < 10 kg) intravenously over 6 hours on day 1/ doxorubicin (30 mg/m 2 /dose or 1 mg/kg/dose for < 10 kg) intravenously over 15 minutes on days 1 and 2/ 5-fluorouracil (600 mg/m 2 /dose or 20 mg/kg/dose for < 10 kg) intravenous push on day 2/ vincristine (1.5 mg/m 2 /day or 0.05 mg/kg/day) intravenous push on days 2, 9, and 16. The cycles of VIT could be adjusted to limit exposure to temsirolimus within 28 days of a major surgical procedure to avoid the risk of thrombosis and poor wound healing. Responders received dexrazoxane (300 mg/m 2 /dose or 10 mg/kg/dose for patients less than 10 kg), intravenous push prior to doxorubicin during the last two cycles of C5VD. All cycles lasted 21 days. Patients who were non-responders received 6 cycles of C5VD with dexrazoxane administered prior to doxorubicin for the final two cycles. Surgery: Patients could have primary tumor resection at any point during therapy, either by surgical resection of orthotopic liver transplant (OLT), optimally after cycle #7 in responders or after cycle #6 in non-responders, to permit for post-surgical chemotherapy. Metastatic lesions were to be addressed surgically at the discretion of treating physicians. Pathology: Central pathologic review was performed for all resected/biopsied specimens (liver and/or lung) to assess tumor histology, surgical margins, microscopic satellite nodules, and microscopic vascular invasion. Toxicity: The individual occurrence of toxicities was graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Toxicity Criteria v 4 guidelines. All Grade 3 or 4 or greater nonhematological toxicities, as well as any toxicity that required submission of an AdEERs report as outlined in the protocol, were to be reported while the patient was on protocol therapy. The frequency of each toxicity type was quantified as the percent of reporting periods on which the toxicity of the relevant grade was reported. All reporting periods where the patient received at least one dose of each of the agents in the therapeutic plan for that individual was included in the denominator for the rate calculation. Statistical Design and Analysis: The primary endpoint was disease status at the end of two cycles of therapy.

Patients were to be considered evaluable if the individual met eligibility criteria, received at least one dose of each agent in the combination being tested, and was not removed from protocol therapy for reasons other than toxicity or disease progression prior to the end of the first cycle of treatment. Any evaluable patient who had a complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) was to be considered as a responder. All other evaluable patients were considered non-responders. The effectiveness of VIT was assessed using a two-stage design that was intended to show an improved response rate compared to the response observed with the initial VI regimen as directed in this trial. In the first stage, 22 patients were to be enrolled. If among the first 22 patients there were 9 or fewer responders, then the trial would be terminated. Otherwise, 19 additional patients would be accrued for a total of 41. If 23 or more of the 41 patients were considered as responders, then the regimen would be considered to have demonstrated sufficient disease control warranting further investigation. If the regimen was associated with a true response rate of 45%, the design would identify the regimen as not sufficiently effective for further development with probability 0.90. If the regimen was associated with a true response rate of 65%, the regimen would be considered of sufficient efficacy to warrant further development with probability 0.90. Evaluation of Response: Baseline physical exams, organ function, AFP levels, and imaging studies, including a CT of the chest, were performed prior to therapy. Additional imaging studies were performed after 2 cycles of VIT and then after every 2 cycles of C5VD. AFP levels were drawn prior to each cycle. For enrollment, metastatic disease was determined by the clinical impression of the treating physician. Response for the primary analysis was assessed using both the RECIST from the central review and the decline in serum AFP levels. The AFP decline during the initial window period was determined using the maximum AFP prior to the initiation of chemotherapy and the last AFP prior to the initiation of cycle #3. Patients who did not have AFP evaluations prior to treatment initiation and/or cycle #3 would be evaluable for RECIST response only in the primary response analysis. Measurable disease was defined as the presence of at least one lesion that could be accurately measured in at least one dimension with the longest diameter at least 20 mm while for chest CT scans, lesions were considered measurable if they were at least 10 mm. Up to 10 measurable lesions were followed for response. RECIST assesses tumor response as the sum of the longest diameter for all target lesions. Non-measurable metastatic disease included all lesions that did not qualify as measurable disease. A complete response (CR) was defined as the disappearance of all target lesions and a normal AFP level. A partial response (PR) was considered as either: 1) At least a 30% decrease in the disease measurement; OR 2) serum AFP level concentration decline of ≥ 90% (1 log 10 ) after two VIT cycles for patients with initially elevated markers in the absence of disease progression by imaging. Progressive disease (PD) was at least a 20% increase in the disease measurement, taking as reference the smallest disease measurement recorded since the start of treatment, or the appearance of one or more new lesions. Patients were to be considered to have stable disease (SD) if they had neither sufficient shrinkage to qualify for PR nor sufficient increase to qualify for (progressive diseases) PD and less than a 90% decline in AFP. Increase in AFP level alone was not considered to be progressive PD. Overall survival (OS) was defined as time from enrollment until death from any cause or last follow-up, whichever came first. The time to event outcome was estimated by the method of Kaplan and Meier with 95% log-log confidence intervals (CI).
