Results Between October 2014 and March 2018, a total of 40 patients were enrolled. Four patients were deemed ineligible, two due to inadequate organ function criteria and two due to disease type/histology. The remaining 36 patients were included in this report. Outcome data current to March 31, 2022, were used in the analysis. The median age at enrollment was 27 months (range: 7 - 170) ( ). There were 25 males and 11 females. All patients had metastatic disease. Only one patient had an AFP < 100 ng/ml at diagnosis. The median AFP at diagnosis was 222,648 ng/ml (range, 71 - 1,524,000). The median AFP following 2 cycles of VIT was 19,262 ng/ml (range, 36 - 450,000). Response: Seventeen of 36 patients (47%) were considered to be responders (RECIST and AFP=3, RECIST only=4, AFP only=10) ( ). Interestingly, one patient was a non-responder and had early progression of both liver and lung disease despite having a 90% decline in AFP. Following the recommendation of the data safety monitoring committee, enrollment was suspended early with 5 potential patient enrollments remaining. The required number of responses to identify VIT as efficacious could not be reached regardless of the results of the 5 additional patients. Therefore, there was no need for further accrual to address the primary endpoint. Among the 32 patients with AFP evaluations during the initial window period, the pattern of change in AFP separated into 2 groups: 5 patients had minimal to no change or a rise in AFP level during window therapy, while the remaining 27 patients had > 50% decline of the AFP ( ). Outcome: Three-year EFS was 47% (95% CI: 30 - 62 %) while overall survival was 67% (95% CI: 49 - 80%) ( ). Eighteen patients had recurrent disease. The sites of recurrence were pulmonary alone in 11 patients, liver alone in 5 patient, and 2 patients had a combined pulmonary and liver recurrence. No patients experienced a toxic death as a first event. Surgery: Twenty-nine patients were able to undergo a tumor resection, including eight who received a liver transplant ( ). Fourteen patients had a pulmonary resection/biopsy in an effort to assess/remove metastatic disease (detailed results to be reported separately). However, a similar pattern of substantial AFP decline not meeting the threshold for the protocol-defined response was observed. In total 27 of the 32 fully evaluable patients (84%) in this report of patients who received VIT had AFP declines greater than 50 percent. For the VIT window the 3-year event-free survival was 47% and the 3-year overall survival was 67%. This is similar to the VI window in which the 3-year EFS rate for the 30 patients who were evaluable for response was 49% (95% CI, 30%-65%) and the 3-year overall survival rate was 62% (95% CI, 42%-77%). It is critically important to note however, that this high-risk study cohort was specifically intended to identify the efficacy of new agents and was not powered to demonstrate differences in outcome. Alternative study designs with larger number of patients would be needed to explore the impact of VI on outcome. Diarrhea and GI toxicity were in the range of previously reported trials and infectious toxicity was less during the VIT cycles than during the C5VD cycles. Based on the similar response and outcome data for VIT compared to VI, it is clear temsirolimus did not enhance the efficacy of VI. However, the additional VIT data does provide important additional evidence for the activity of irinotecan-based chemotherapy in treating HB. Combining the two strata, 66 patients in total were treated with irinotecan-based regimens. Although the overall protocol-defined response rate for these two strata was 47% (31/66), the percentage of patients who had greater than a 90% decline in AFP after two cycles of treatment was 36% (24/66) while a change in RECIST occurred in 16 of 66 (24%) patients suggesting that AFP may be a more sensitive indicator of disease response than RECIST. Importantly, this was the COG first clinical trial to use AFP as a prospective indicator of response and study guided therapeutic decisions. While the overall change in AFP from diagnosis to the completion of 4 cycles and to the completion of therapy has been shown to be prognostic in previous trials, the rate of decline has yet to demonstrate prognosis in a clinical trial. A separate paper looking at AFP responses in the entire AHEP0731 cohort is in preparation as this is the largest prospective collection of AFP data in a treatment trial of HB. In summary, the VIT regimen did not meet protocol-defined criteria for demonstrating sufficient disease control to be considered successful. A closer examination of the percentage decline in serum AFP levels demonstrated that VIT, similar to the VI regimen, did appear to have activity in a large group of newly diagnosed patients with high-risk HB. Treatment was tolerated with reasonable toxicity. Although, the addition of temsirolimus to VI did not provide evidence of enhanced activity when compared to VI in up front window therapy, the VIT strata did provide additional evidence for the efficacy and tolerability of irinotecan-based regimens in treating high-risk HB. The VI and VIT regimens suggest activity of irinotecan in newly diagnosed patients supporting results seen in previous trials of patients with relapsed HB. The currently enrolling PHITT AHEP1531 trial uses VI as part of an intensified consolidation therapy for high-risk HB patients who do not achieve a complete response to induction therapy. The exact role of VI in treating HB in both newly diagnosed and recurrent patients is yet to be defined and will need to be evaluated in prospective trials designed to explore the impact of this therapy on survival.
